pronunciation.t: ع (ayn) is a deep throaty sound
pronunciation.tip: Tighten your throat like swallowing in reverse: عَرب (ʿarab) = Arab.

pronunciation.t: ح (ḥa) is a breathy deep H
pronunciation.tip: Breathe hard from deep in the throat: حَب (ḥabb) = love.

pronunciation.t: خ (kha) scrapes like clearing your throat
ق (qaf) is a deep K from the back
pronunciation.tip: K made far back in the throat: قَلب (qalb) = heart.

pronunciation.t: ث and ذ are soft TH sounds
pronunciation.tip: ث like THINK (ثلاثة = three), ذ like THIS (ذهب = gold).

alphabet.title: The Arabic alphabet
alphabet.explain: Arabic has 28 letters, written right-to-left. Letters change shape at the start, middle and end of words — but the sounds stay the same. Learn sounds first, shapes second!

counting.title: Counting 0 to 100
counting.explain: Numbers 1–10 first, then 11–19 (ones + عشر), then tens to 100. 21 = واحد وعشرون (one and twenty) — ones come FIRST!
rules: 21+ puts ones FIRST: واحد وعشرون = 21 (one-and-twenty). Tens end in -ون: عشرون، ثلاثون.

lessons.title: Greetings: السلام عليكم
lessons.learn: The famous greeting! السلام عليكم (peace upon you) → answer وعليكم السلام (and upon you peace). Morning: صباح الخير → answer صباح النور! Greetings always come in PAIRS.

grammar.title: Greetings come in pairs
grammar.explain: السلام عليكم → وعليكم السلام. صباح الخير → صباح النور (morning of light!). مساء الخير → مساء النور. Never answer a greeting with the same greeting — use its PAIR!
mistakes: Answering السلام عليكم with السلام عليكم — reply وعليكم السلام!
Saying صباح الخير at night — evenings need مساء الخير!

dialogue.en: And upon you peace! Good morning!

lessons.title: Names and how are you
lessons.learn: اسمي ليلى = My name is Layla. Ask: ما اسمك؟ (m) / ما اسمكِ؟ (f) — -KA for men, -KI for women! How are you: كيف حالك؟ → بخير، الحمد لله (fine, praise God)!

grammar.title: -ka (m) / -ki (f): your
grammar.explain: اسمكَ (ismuka) = your name (to a man), اسمكِ (ismukī) = your name (to a woman). حالكَ/حالكِ the same. اسمي = MY name (works for everyone). Check who you talk to — pick -KA or -KI!
mistakes: Saying اسمك to a woman — women get اسمكِ (-KI)!
Forgetting الحمد لله after بخير — it always follows!

lessons.title: Thank you, please, sorry: the polite three
lessons.learn: Three words carry almost every small exchange: شكراً (thank you), عفواً (you're welcome — and also 'excuse me'), and من فضلك (please). They change with the person you speak to: من فضلكِ and تفضّلي to a woman, آسفة if you are the woman apologising.

grammar.title: Politeness follows gender
grammar.pattern: min faḍlik → min faḍlik(i) · āsif → āsifa · tafaḍḍal → tafaḍḍalī
grammar.explain: Arabic marks the person you are addressing, not your own politeness. To a man: من فضلك، تفضّل. To a woman: من فضلكِ، تفضّلي. If you are a woman apologising, you say آسفة.

mistakes.why: The word شكراً ends in an alif; it takes no extra ending for the person addressed.
The feminine ending is a kasra, not a ي: فضلكِ.

lessons.title: Gender: هذا / هذه
lessons.learn: Two genders! هذا = this (m), هذه = this (f). Feminine usually ends in ة (ta marbuta): مدرسة (school-f), سيارة (car-f). No ة? Usually masculine: كتاب (book-m), بيت (house-m)!

grammar.title: هذا (m) / هذه (f) + ة
grammar.explain: هذا كتاب (this is a book-m), هذه مدرسة (this is a school-f). Adjectives match: رجل كبير (big man), امرأة كبيرة (big woman) — feminine adds ة!
mistakes: Saying هذا مدرسة — ة-words need هذه!
Saying امرأة كبير — feminine needs كبيرة!

dialogue.en: Yes, this is a big book.

lessons.title: Plurals: كتاب → كتب
lessons.learn: Plurals transform! Sound feminine: سيارة → سيارات (add -ات). People masculine: مدرس → مدرسون (-ون). And BROKEN plurals reshape the word: كتاب → كتب, قلم → أقلام. Learn each word WITH its plural!

grammar.title: Three plural roads
grammar.explain: سيارة→سيارات (-ات for most feminine). مدرس→مدرسون (-ون for male people). Broken: كتاب→كتب, قلم→أقلام, بيت→بيوت — memorise the pair!
mistakes: Saying كتابات — books are broken: كتب!
Saying مدرسات for male teachers — men take -ون!

lessons.title: Counting to five: one, two, three, كم؟
lessons.learn: كم (how many) turns numbers into questions: كم كتاباً عندك؟ A number from three to ten takes a plural noun — ثلاثة كتب — but one and two sit directly on the noun, and two even changes its shape.

grammar.title: Numbers and the noun
grammar.pattern: three to ten + plural · one/two + singular (two uses the dual)
grammar.explain: ثلاثة كتب، خمسة طلاب. One and two behave differently: كتاب واحد، كتابان (dual). After كم the counted noun is singular accusative in careful Arabic: كم كتاباً عندك؟

examples.en: How many students are in the class?
In the bag there are five books.

mistakes.why: Two is expressed by the dual form of the noun, not by اثنان + plural.
Numbers three to ten take a plural noun.

dialogue.en: How many books do you have?
I have three books, and this is a fourth.
And how many brothers do you have?
I have one brother and two sisters.

lessons.title: I have: عندي
lessons.learn: عندي = I have (at-me)! عندك (you-m have), عندها (she has). فِي = there is: في البيت (in the house). عندي كتاب = I have a book. Swap endings, own everything!

grammar.title: عندي + thing = I have
grammar.explain: عندي كتاب (I have a book), عندك ماء؟ (do you have water?), ما عندي وقت (I have no time — ما negates!). فِي for places: الكتاب في البيت (the book is in the house).
mistakes: Saying أنا أملك first — natives say عندي!
Saying لا عندي — negate with ما: ما عندي!

lessons.title: Asking: ما، من، أين، هل
lessons.learn: Four question makers cover most of A1: ما (what), من (who), أين (where) and هل for any yes/no question. They stand at the front, and the rest of the sentence does not move.

grammar.title: Questions keep the sentence order
grammar.pattern: question word + subject + verb · hal + statement
grammar.explain: Arabic does not reorder for questions. ما اسمك؟ is literally 'what your-name?'. هل turns a statement into a yes/no question with no other change: أنت طالب → هل أنت طالب؟

mistakes.why: ما is already a question; هل is only for yes/no questions.
The question word stays at the front: من أين أنت؟

culture.text: Greetings in the Arab world come in pairs and carry religion, warmth and time: السلام عليكم is answered وعليكم السلام, and a visitor is offered coffee or tea before business. Refusing the cup is read as refusing the welcome, so a small sip is the polite minimum. The same page teaches fuṣḥā, the shared written Arabic; on the street you will also hear a local dialect — both are Arabic, not one right and one wrong.

reading.text: اسمي منى. أنا من عمّان، وأسكن في القاهرة. صباح الخير! كيف حالك؟ أنا بخير، الحمد لله. هذا صديقي، اسمه كريم. هو طالب في الجامعة. عندي درس الآن، مع السلامة!
reading.gloss: My name is Mona. I am from Amman and I live in Cairo. Good morning! How are you? I am fine, praise God. This is my friend, his name is Karim. He is a student at the university. I have a class now — goodbye!

listening.script:
أ: صباح الخير! كيف حالك؟
ب: بخير، شكراً. وأنت؟
أ: بخير، الحمد لله.
ب: هذا كتاب جديد؟
أ: نعم، هذا كتاب عربي.
listening.gloss: A: Good morning! How are you? B: Fine, thanks. And you? A: Fine, praise God. B: Is this a new book? A: Yes, this is an Arabic book.

idioms.meaning: the standard greeting; answered وعليكم السلام
said to praise something without envy
about the future; softens any promise
the default answer to كيف حالك
welcome — said to a guest arriving
with pleasure; a warm yes to a small request
at your service, especially to a customer
you are welcome — it was my duty
said when someone eats or drinks

mistakes.why: Arabic marks the subject in the verb or pronoun; doubling أنا sounds like a stutter.
مرحبا is fine alone, but the paired greeting uses السلام عليكم.
طالبة is feminine, so the demonstrative must be هذه.

task.title: Your first meeting, out loud
task.instructions: Record a 30-second self-introduction in Arabic script first, then read it aloud: greeting, name, city, one thing you have (عندي), and a goodbye. Reread the culture note and use its pair-answer for the greeting rather than echoing it.
